inspection_summary: Inspected all 1,974 lines. This panoramic review develops several distinct semantic bridges between zeta data and physics: the explicit formula and zero-density expansion turn primes into periodic-orbit-like oscillations; classical escape and trace formulas make RH-sensitive corrections observable in principle; quantum scattering, xp, inverse-potential, and Hilbert-Polya models expose both spectral possibilities and recurrent failures to reproduce the oscillatory term; random-matrix statistics constrain symmetry while retaining system-specific long-range corrections; and lattice, Bose-gas, primon-gas, spectral-zeta, and Brownian constructions translate poles, zeros, factorization, and Moebius sums into physical observables. The two-column extraction often interleaves sections and degrades formulas, but the prose mechanisms and their stated limitations remain recoverable.

inspection_summary: Inspected all 1,515 lines. The paper proves a multidimensional Selberg central limit theorem at mesoscopic shifts, derives an exotic Gaussian law for zero-count fluctuations, and establishes the exact random-matrix analogue under n corresponding to log t. Its proof architecture is itself reusable: logarithms of characteristic polynomials become trace-power series controlled by Diaconis-Evans; log zeta becomes a short prime Dirichlet polynomial through Selberg's explicit-formula approximation; Montgomery-Vaughan controls the tail; slow growth plus unique factorization converts time averages to independent torus averages; and matched covariance lemmas in the two settings yield the same min-kernel. A branching-tree construction finally makes positivity and the hierarchical covariance structure transparent.

inspection_summary: Inspected the complete hash-matching normalized file. The frozen assignment declares 912 lines, but the file has only 909 physical lines; lines 910-912 are therefore explicitly covered as extraction-defective rather than supplied from elsewhere. The paper reformulates Nyman-Beurling in a smaller symmetry-defined Hilbert space with an explicit sine-difference orthonormal basis. It proves that RH is equivalent to approximating the first basis vector by fractional-part differences, computes all relevant coordinates, and studies triangular, natural Moebius, and smoothed approximations. In each case coordinatewise convergence is established, while the remaining obstacle is a square-summable uniform dominator on a finite moving range; the natural approximation also exposes a restrictive Moebius-sum obstruction, and smoothing gives a criterion known under RH to achieve a quantitative rate.
